title: Ho and the Baby Eater: Glossary and Pronunciation Guide
description: A spoiler-light reader aid for recurring names, atua, places, peoples, Polynesian terms, and in-world words from Ho & the Baby Eater.
authorNote: The language choices in this manuscript are governed, where possible, by POLLEX, the Polynesian Lexicon Project Online: a comparative dictionary of Polynesian languages that gathers cognates, reflexes, and reconstructed older forms. My aim is not to decorate English prose with isolated Polynesian words, but to make the world think, name, worship, judge, remember, and misunderstand itself through language closer to pre-colonial contact.

That choice is deliberate and carries a cost. A modern English-language novelist has access to a vast working inheritance: major dictionaries record hundreds of thousands of English words and phrases, and an educated adult writer can draw on tens of thousands of known words before even reaching for specialist vocabulary. POLLEX is invaluable, but it is a narrower tool for a different job. Once forms are filtered for pre-contact plausibility, cultural fit, part of speech, semantic precision, sound, and story context, the usable pool of nouns and verbs becomes much smaller.

This limitation shaped the prose. Sometimes a scene could not simply use the first English word that came to mind; it had to be rebuilt around a concept that had an older Polynesian pathway, or around a moral category that belonged more naturally to the world of the story. Terms such as mana, tapu, utu, wairua, atua, rohe, and rāhui are therefore not interchangeable ornaments. They are part of the book’s architecture: its cosmology, belief system, social order, ethics, and sense of consequence.

Note: This is a story-facing language note, not a formal linguistic apparatus. Pronunciation guidance is approximate and designed to help global readers move through the journal chapters with confidence.

pronunciationGuide.title: Vowels
body: Māori and most Polynesian languages share a consistent vowel system. Once the sounds below are learned, any word in this glossary can be sounded out more reliably.
i — as in feet, but shorter
u — as in moon, but shorter

pronunciationGuide.title: Macrons (ā ē ī ō ū)
body: A macron lengthens the vowel. It roughly doubles the duration without changing the vowel quality: ā is a held “ah.” Ō is a held “oh,” sounding like “awe” as in awestruck.
Macrons can change meaning as well as pronunciation, so they are part of the word rather than decoration.

pronunciationGuide.title: Diphthongs
body: Two vowels blend smoothly together without a break.
ae → ah-eh ai → ah-ee ao → ah-oh au → ah-oo
ei → eh-ee oe → oh-eh oi → oh-ee ou → oh-oo

pronunciationGuide.title: Consonants
body: Most consonants are close to English, with three key differences:
r — a light flap, closer to the r in Spanish pero than the English r
ng — always the sound in singing, never as in finger; it can begin a syllable
wh — pronounced as f in most Māori dialects, as in whakapapa → fah-kah-PAH-pah

pronunciationGuide.title: Stress
body: Stress generally falls on the first syllable. Macronned vowels draw additional weight wherever they appear.
The pronunciations in brackets use a plain-English respelling. Syllables are separated by hyphens and stressed syllables appear in CAPS.

entries.wider: mana can also mean prestige, authority, status, spiritual force, or personal power.
